The reproductive biology of Asiatic toad (Bufo gargarizans) has been documented under controlled thermal conditions in the laboratory. Females maintained at a constant water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] produce between approximately 5000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5000 eggs per spawning event], with a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year]. Embryonic development proceeds relatively rapidly under these thermal conditions, with hatching occurring approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] after egg deposition at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This short embryonic period, broadly consistent with values reported for nearctic congeners such as Anaxyrus americanus, suggests that thermal conditions represent a major determinant of early ontogenetic pace in this species. The size of newly hatched larvae is modest, with each neonate weighing a mere 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] upon emergence from the egg capsule.

As the free-swimming tadpoles progress through the larval phase, they undergo a dramatic metamorphic transformation that culminates in the transition to a terrestrial body plan. By the completion of metamorphosis, the total length at metam reaches approximately 3.5 centimeters , a size reflecting the morphological changes of tail resorption and limb development that characterise the climax of amphibian larval metamorphosis. This metamorphic size is comparable to that recorded for the closely related common toad Bufo bufo, from which the estimate is derived. Following successful metamorphosis, the newly terrestrial toadlets enter a period of accelerated somatic growth. During this juvenile phase, individuals feed actively on small arthropods and accumulate body mass. Ultimately, under optimal conditions, adults reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 250 grams [Wwi = approximately 250 grams] and females achieve a maximum size that defines their reproductive capacity.

Sexual maturation in Bufo gargarizans exhibits a clear difference between the sexes, a pattern commonly observed in bufonids with male-biased reproductive competition. Under a thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], females attain puberty at a time since birth at puberty for females of approximately 1095 days [tp = approximately 1095 days], whereas males develop much more rapidly, achieving reproductive maturity at a time since birth at puberty for males of only about 730 days [tp = about 730 days]. This earlier maturation in males is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises early access to breeding opportunities, a pattern intensified by the male-biased operational sex ratios that characterise many explosive-breeding anurans. The difference of over a year in the timing of sexual maturation likely has significant consequences for the demography and mating system of this population.

The overall body size attained by adult toads reflects both the prolonged growth period and the energetic demands of reproduction. Maximum body size in female Bufo gargarizans is attained over several years, with adult females reaching an ultimate total length for females of 12.5 centimeters [Li = 12.5 centimeters]. Males, by contrast, are distinctly smaller, with an ultimate total length for males of 11.5 centimeters [Li = 11.5 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, in which females surpass males by roughly one centimeter in snout–vent length, is typical of bufonid toads and is thought to arise from fecundity selection favouring larger body size in females, which can accommodate a greater number of ova. Correspondingly, the maximum reproductive rate estimated for females is substantial. Observations from captive populations kept at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] indicate a daily reproductive output of approximately 13.7 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 13.7 eggs per day] when averaged over the entire breeding season.

Under the constant thermal conditions of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] that appear to approximate optimal developmental temperatures for this species, the complete lifespan of Bufo gargarizans is estimated to be approximately 24.2 years [am = approximately 24.2 years]. This substantial longevity—more than two decades under favourable conditions—is a notable feature of the species' life history, distinguishing it from many smaller-bodied anurans that complete their life cycles in just a few years. The extended lifespan allows multiple reproductive events over the course of an individual's life, providing repeated opportunities for successful breeding. The combination of a relatively large body size, delayed maturation in females, and a prolonged reproductive window suggests that Bufo gargarizans occupies a comparatively slow end of the life-history continuum among Asian bufonids, with high adult survival buffering the population against stochastic fluctuations in recruitment success from year to year.
